The lesion had appeared without an identifiable cause. For the previous 2 months, the patient had applied topical corticosteroids and antifungals with no improvement.

clinical_record:
A 34‐year‐old African American man with hemophilia A, HIV‐1 infection, and hepatitis C virus infection presented with a 3‐month history of intermittent fever, unintentional weight loss, and progressive lip swelling with painful ulcerations. Six months earlier he had resumed antiretroviral therapy, with his CD4 count rising from 94 to 160 cells/mm3; the lip lesions developed approximately two months after the CD4 count began to improve. He had received multiple courses of antibiotics and systemic corticosteroids without benefit. He was taking acyclovir for herpes simplex prophylaxis and dapsone for Pneumocystis jiroveci prophylaxis. 

On examination, his lips were markedly edematous, with multiple superficial ulcers having heaped‐up margins. There was no hepatosplenomegaly. The initial differential diagnosis included herpetic ulcers, bacterial infection, fungal infection, and angioedema. 

Diagnostic studies showed an undetectable HIV viral load and undetectable hepatitis C viral load. A polymerase‐chain‐reaction assay for herpes simplex virus from an ulcer base was negative. Complement C1 esterase inhibitor levels were within normal limits. Gram stain, acid‐fast stain, and mucicarmine stain of lesion samples were negative. Fungal blood cultures and both urine and serum Histoplasma antigen tests were negative.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
reference_diagnosis: Histoplasmosis

clinical_record:
A 32-year-old Caucasian woman presents with severe left knee pain and bilateral genu valgum deformity. She recalls being told she “may have had rickets” at age 9 but was lost to follow-up. At 22, she had trochanteric bursitis and an X-ray showed a Q-angle of 17°; no metabolic evaluation was done. She takes OTC vitamin D3 without calcium. She is 155 cm tall, weighs 58.5 kg (BMI 23.8), with no personal or family history of fractures or metabolic bone disease.

On exam, there is marked bilateral valgus alignment (left > right) with a knocking gait. Repeat X-ray shows a Q-angle of 23°. Bone density scanning reveals osteopenia of the left femoral head and normal lumbar spine density. Laboratory studies show:
• Serum phosphate: low  
• Total 25-hydroxyvitamin D and 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D: elevated  
• Parathyroid hormone: low  
• FGF23: undetectable  

A 24-hour urine collection demonstrates inappropriately normal phosphate excretion for the degree of hypophosphatemia and normal urine calcium. Renal ultrasound reveals bilateral medullary nephrocalcinosis without stones.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
reference_diagnosis: Hereditary hypophosphatemic rickets with hypercalciuria

clinical_record:
A 39-year-old man with a history of treated tuberculosis presented with two weeks of fever, generalized weakness, vague abdominal pain, vomiting, headache, body aches, and moderate nasal bleeding. On examination, he had a 2×1 cm submandibular lymph node and hepatomegaly (7 cm below the costal margin), without gastrointestinal symptoms or skin lesions. Laboratory studies showed urea 18.8 mmol/L, creatinine 141 µmol/L, lipase 182 U/L, myoglobin 108 ng/mL, ferritin >40 000 µg/L, vitamin B12 <111 pmol/L, normal fibrinogen, and triglycerides. Viral serologies were negative. Complete blood count revealed pancytopenia: hemoglobin 6.4 g/dL, WBC 1.7×10^3/µL, ANC 0.9×10^3/µL, platelets 2×10^3/µL. Head CT showed bilateral subdural hemorrhages without midline shift. Whole-body CT demonstrated bilateral pleural effusion, extensive pulmonary consolidation, thrombosis of the celiac artery with splenic infarction, mild hepatomegaly, and massive splenomegaly with infarction. 

Initial peripheral smear showed very few atypical cells; a repeat smear revealed marked leukopenia and 13% abnormal blastoid cells of medium size with fine nuclear chromatin, unevenly distributed coarse basophilic granules, and occasional bilobed nuclei. Bone marrow aspirate was hypercellular with 26% immature metachromatic blasts—cells with eccentric nuclei, abundant cytoplasm, and coarse giant granules—as well as some agranular high N/C blasts and spindle-shaped cells. There was trilineage dysplasia with megaloblastic changes in granulocytes and erythroid precursors, dysplastic megakaryocytes, and frequent mitoses. Both histiocytes and the atypical cells demonstrated erythrophagocytosis.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
reference_diagnosis: mast cell leukaemia

A 34-year-old Thai man with a history of hypertension and tobacco use disorder, and a family history significant for polycythemia, hypertension, and stroke in his father. He initially presented with worsening bifrontal headaches, nausea, vomiting, and right-sided blurry vision. He was not adherent to his antihypertensive regimen. Three months later, he presented again with right-sided frontal headache, photophobia, tingling in his right fingers, nausea, and vomiting. He reported missing a few doses of his carvedilol and had cut down on his smoking.

Blood pressures in the emergency department ranged from 180 to 190/80-90 mm Hg during initial presentation. On second presentation, systolic blood pressures were 150 to 170 mm Hg. National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale score was 2 because of complete left homonymous hemianopsia.

Erythropoietin was normal (7.8 mIU/mL).- Imaging studies:  - CT Head: Left occipital intraparenchymal hemorrhage with intravascular extension (first presentation)  - CT Head: Right posterior parietal intraparenchymal hemorrhage (4.7 × 2.9 × 4.2 cm) with blood product in the right lateral ventricle and minimal midline shift (second presentation)  - MRI Brain: No underlying masses  - Peripheral smear: Showed microcytosis and thrombocytopenia without toxic granulations or blast cells- Hemoglobin Electrophoresis Results:  Hb A: 0.0%  Hb F: 1.7%  Hb A2: 4.4%  Hb E: 34.0%  Hb Tak: 59.9%

clinical_record:
A 71-year-old woman with a history of type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and ischemic heart disease presented with a 2-month history of intermittent painless hematuria with passage of clots. She denied dysuria, frequency, or other lower urinary tract symptoms, and there was no family history of malignancy. On examination, vital signs and abdominal and pelvic exams were unremarkable. Laboratory evaluation showed a hemoglobin level of 8.6 g/dL requiring blood transfusion; serum creatinine and other biochemical parameters were within normal limits. Transabdominal ultrasonography revealed a 2.9 × 2.5 × 2.4 cm polypoidal mass arising from the posterolateral wall of the bladder dome; both kidneys and the upper tracts appeared normal. Pre- and postvoid bladder volumes were 180 mL and 44 mL, respectively. Cystoscopy demonstrated an exophytic solid tumor measuring 1.5 × 2.0 cm on the anterior fundal wall, covered with slough. A deep transurethral resection of the bladder tumor was performed. Histopathological analysis revealed an adenocarcinoma composed of mucinous and signet-ring cell components. Thus, a secondary adenocarcinoma or a rare variant of primary adenocarcinoma of the bladder was suspected.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
reference_diagnosis: Primary signet-ring cell carcinoma of the bladder
